articles.title: Claude Code's engine, packaged as a library
articles.summary: Why the Claude Agent SDK isn't a Messages API wrapper, but Claude Code embeddable in your own application

subsections.title: Not just another way to call the API

blocks.content: The Claude Agent SDK exposes the same agentic engine the Claude Code CLI uses — context management, tool execution, permissions, automatic compaction, hooks — to embed it directly into a Python or TypeScript application. It isn't a convenience layer over `POST /v1/messages`: it's Claude Code packaged as a library, with the entire harness that makes it autonomous already solved.

blocks.title: Quick rule of thumb
blocks.content: A single stateless call? Messages API. An autonomous agent with persistent context, running inside your own infrastructure? Agent SDK. The same thing without operating the infrastructure yourself? Managed Agents. Direct interactive human use in a terminal? Claude Code as-is.

subsections.title: Python and TypeScript, with near-total parity

blocks.content: The SDK ships as two independent packages — one for Python, one for TypeScript/Node.js — exposing the same conceptual surface (`query()`, `options`, message types, hooks, subagents). Neither wraps the other: each is a native implementation in its own language, meant to integrate with the rest of that application's code without a translation layer.

blocks.title: They aren't 100% identical
blocks.content: The TypeScript SDK picks up certain events and options before the Python one does — for example, some hook types or direct access to the initial `session_id` (`message.session_id`) are simpler in TypeScript, while in Python they're nested inside `message.data`. Check the specific SDK's reference before porting code between the two rather than assuming full parity.

articles.title: Packages and requirements
articles.summary: The real package names for Python and TypeScript, and how both bundle the Claude Code binary with no separate install

blocks.code:
# Python (requires 3.10+)
pip install claude-agent-sdk

# TypeScript / Node.js
npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk

blocks.title: The CLI ships bundled
blocks.content: Both packages bundle the native Claude Code binary — most installs don't need to install the CLI separately or already have it present on the system.

The SDK reuses the same credential mechanism as Claude Code: a Claude API key via the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` environment variable, or whatever session Claude Code already has configured on that machine. It doesn't introduce a separate authentication system of its own.

articles.title: The agentic loop the SDK handles for you
articles.summary: query() as the entry point, and what a custom loop over the Messages API gets solved automatically

blocks.content: The main function is `query(prompt, options)`, which returns an async generator of messages. Internally it runs the full cycle: Claude evaluates the situation, requests tool calls, receives the results, and repeats until done — without your code having to manually parse `tool_use` blocks or hand-build the next turn with `tool_result`.

rows: Context accumulation across turns, no reset
Implicit — no need to rebuild history on every call
Compaction as context approaches the limit

blocks.title: `bypassPermissions` is a real SDK value, not a recommendation
blocks.content: It's one of the documented `permissionMode` values — it auto-approves any tool call that reaches that step in the evaluation chain (see the permissions pipeline in this site's Permissions section). Using it carries the same risk as disabling any approval gate: it's an explicit design decision for cases where the environment is already isolated or the risk is acceptable, not a default to reach for without thinking.

The async generator returned by `query()` emits typed messages. Telling them apart is what lets you react to each stage of the loop — showing progress, logging cost, detecting the final result — instead of treating everything as plain text.

rows: At session start and on lifecycle events (subtypes `init`, `compact_boundary`, `informational`, `worker_shutting_down`)
After every Claude response, including the final one with no tool calls
After a tool runs, when its result goes back to the model
Raw API streaming events: text deltas, tool input chunks
When the loop ends — always the last message

blocks.title: Access differs slightly between SDKs
blocks.content: Python distinguishes messages with `isinstance(message, AssistantMessage)` and reaches `message.content` directly. TypeScript checks `message.type === "assistant"` and the content sits one level deeper, at `message.message.content`.

The SDK supports the same hooks as the Claude Code CLI — `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `SubagentStart`, `SubagentStop`, `PreCompact` — configured as callbacks in `options.hooks` instead of as external scripts in `settings.json`. They run in the host application's process, not inside the agent's context window, so they don't consume context tokens.

rows: Resume the most recent session without tracking its ID
Resume a specific saved session, even from another machine if a custom `sessionStore` is used
Create a new branch of the session without altering the original

articles.title: What the SDK ships with by default
articles.summary: The SDK doesn't start empty: it includes an already-implemented tool set, restrictable via allowedTools

rows: ToolSearch — loads MCP tools on demand instead of all upfront

subsections.title: Restricting the set with allowedTools / disallowedTools

blocks.content: They're restricted with `options.allowedTools` (an array of strings), which supports wildcards like `"mcp__server-name__*"` to enable every tool from a specific MCP server at once. `options.disallowedTools` does the opposite: it blocks specific tools without having to re-enumerate the rest of the allowed set.

blocks.title: Nothing gets added automatically
blocks.content: The default set doesn't grow automatically when an MCP server connects — its tools become available but stay subject to the same `allowedTools`/`disallowedTools` rules as the SDK's native tools.

articles.title: Connecting MCP servers and defining subagents programmatically
articles.summary: Three ways to connect MCP from the SDK, and why the programmatic subagent definition is already covered in depth elsewhere on this site

rows: Local MCP server, as a child process
The server runs inside the same process, no separate subprocess — useful for exposing your own functions as MCP tools without the overhead of an external process

blocks.content: Programmatic subagent definitions via `AgentDefinition` go beyond name, prompt, and tools. The main fields:

rows: Tells the parent agent when to invoke this subagent automatically
If omitted, inherits every tool available to subagents
Excludes specific tools, with support for MCP patterns (`mcp__server__*`)
An alias (`'sonnet'`, `'opus'`, `'inherit'`) or a full model ID
Preloads specific skills when the subagent starts
MCP servers available to that specific subagent
Whether it runs as a non-blocking task (default: `true`)
Controls the tool permission mode for that subagent

blocks.title: Also covered in the Subagents section
blocks.content: General subagent behavior (automatic invocation by description, only a summary returning to the parent) is already documented with examples in this site's Subagents section — this covers specifically the `AgentDefinition` fields as configured from the SDK.

Each subagent runs in its own conversation, isolated from the parent's — it starts fresh unless `fork` is used. Intermediate results from the subagent never leave that isolated conversation; only the final response returns to the parent, as the result of the tool call that invoked it. When several tasks are independent of each other, subagents run in parallel and the whole set finishes in the time of the slowest one, not the sum of all of them.
